songs.title: The Map That Wouldn't Fold
lines: The corner shop was closing when I found the paper map,
Its edges smelled of coffee, with a river through a gap.
The street I needed wasn't where the printed lines had been,
A baker drew a shortcut with a thumb of flour and ink.
I took the eastern staircase past a mural in the rain,
A bicycle mechanic shouted not to trust the lane.
The shutters made a rhythm and the drains began to sing,
I matched the rattling metal with the coins inside my sling.
A taxi splashed the crossing, so I sheltered by a wall,
Its faded movie poster held a number I could call.
I rang. A quiet voice replied, "The bridge is closed till dawn."
I asked about the footpath; they said, "That one isn't gone."
A narrow wooden walkway curved behind the railway line,
Where someone painted arrows that the weather couldn't find.
I followed them till water rose around the gravel bend,
Then stopped beneath a lantern where the footpath seemed to end.
A woman with a shopping bag was waiting by a gate,
She said, "The river changed its course. The paper's out of date."
She showed me where the current left a hollow in the sand,
And lent me one small flashlight I could hold in either hand.
I crossed a little higher where the stones were broad and dry,
The railway bridge above me turned the rain to silver lines.
The house I came to find was standing quietly beyond,
Its windows faced an orchard and a narrow duckweed pond.
A letter in my pocket held a name I hadn't said,
I placed it in the mailbox painted chipped and faded red.
The map was still unfolded when I made the journey back,
And every road looked different with a meaning that it lacked.
I drew a careful footbridge where the printed road was wrong,
And left a space for changes that would come before too long.
No chorus from the heavens, no applause along the trail,
Just one delivered letter, and a map that told the tale.

songs.title: The Mayor of Lost Umbrellas
lines: The mayor of lost umbrellas made a speech about the rain,
Declared the city's pavements needed every drop explained.
He called the council chambers to an emergency parade,
Where every missing umbrella was a missing vote he made.
The treasurer found a yellow one beneath the market floor,
The clerk brought twelve old handles, but no fabric anymore.
A pigeon took the minutes while a lamppost held the chair,
The mayor waved a raincoat like a flag above the square.
"Oh bring them back, those wandering roofs," the weary people cried,
"We've had enough of puddles and our socks have never dried."
The mayor ordered signposts pointing north toward the sea,
A forecast told him clouds don't always follow policy.
A child arrived on Tuesday with a cart of broken sticks,
And asked the council whether they could help her make them fix.
The mayor drew a diagram with arrows and a crown,
But couldn't turn a single bent umbrella right side down.
The child produced a needle, some waterproofing and twine,
She fixed the broken spokes in less than half a lunchtime.
A dozen people gathered, each with something they could mend,
An engineer was holding tape; a cobbler brought a friend.
"Oh bring them back, those wandering roofs," the people sang again,
"Or teach us how to mend one when we're standing in the rain."
By Friday every market stall had opened up a bench,
They charged a button or a joke, or sometimes nothing spent.
The mayor cut the ribbon in his stiff official suit,
A sudden gust went whistling and carried off his boot.
He ran beneath the nearest shade to shelter from the spray,
The child handed him a blue umbrella she'd repaired that day.
The mayor thanked the people, then retired his grand decree,
And passed a law for public benches underneath each tree.
"Oh bring them back" became "We'll fix what's broken here,"
As thunder rolled above the shops, the crowd began to cheer.

songs.title: A Small Blue Frequency
lines: I heard your voice between the stations of the radio,
A little blue frequency beneath the winter snow.
The signal came and vanished when the heater turned to red,
I left the kettle waiting and the lamp beside the bed.
I used to know the numbers you would call to make me smile,
The postcards in the hallway have been there a little while.
I turned the dial so slowly that the static sounded warm,
And listened for a melody inside the passing storm.
Stay, little signal, stay where I can hear,
One note across the distance can make the dark seem clear.
Stay, little signal, don't promise what you can't,
Just light the empty spaces with the music that you can.
The radio kept slipping to a weather report at two,
A warning for the crossing and the northern avenue.
I wrote it on a paper, placed it next to my old shoes,
Then carried extra blankets to the shelter near the school.
The room was full of people who had nowhere else to go,
A girl was teaching dominoes, a grandfather moved slow.
We found a working speaker and we played a local tune,
The smallest kids were dancing under paper stars and moons.
Stay, little signal, stay where we can hear,
One note across the distance can make the dark seem clear.
Stay, little signal, don't promise what you can't,
Just light the empty spaces with the music that you can.
By morning all the roadways were beginning to reopen,
The heater lost its rattle and the curtains caught the sun.
The voice I thought I'd recognized was someone I had known,
Not quite the person I was missing, still a sound that felt like home.
I turned the dial toward the station playing songs before the news,
And left it for the neighbors as they folded up their shoes.
Stay, little signal, go wherever kindness goes,
And carry every weathered voice through sunlight and through snow.

songs.title: Two Apprentices and One Clock
lines: MARA: You tighten every spring until the wheel refuses time.
ELI: And you loosen every bearing till the hands forget their line.
MARA: The clock's a thing of balance, not a trophy made of brass.
ELI: It needs to make the journey if the minutes are to pass.
MARA: I want to take the cover off and check the damaged gear.
ELI: I want to listen first and find the sound that brought us here.
MARA: You waste an hour listening while the customer's away.
ELI: You waste a hundred screws by fixing parts that want to stay.
MARA: Then give me half a minute; hold the lantern to the back.
ELI: And I'll record the ticking as it travels down the rack.
MARA: The second hand is catching on the smallest silver tooth.
ELI: The rhythm that I'm hearing says the spring is slipping loose.
MARA: You're right about the spring; the tooth was only where it froze.
ELI: And you're right that we should open it before the shop is closed.
MARA: I'll keep the pieces sorted by their number and their shape.
ELI: I'll label every resting spot with pencil marks and tape.
MARA: Two hands to hold the balance; one hand can't do it right.
ELI: Two ears to hear a silence in the middle of the night.
MARA: I'll give the wheel a fraction more of room beside its pin.
ELI: I'll wind the spring just once and listen as it starts again.
MARA: The first strike sounds uneven.
ELI: Now the second's coming clean.
MARA: The minute hand is moving.
ELI: And the little gear is seen.
MARA: The owner came for punctuality; we found another art.
ELI: The timepiece needed knowledge from two differently tuned hearts.
MARA: I'll write a note explaining all the changes that we made.
ELI: And I'll set it by the window where the afternoon has stayed.
MARA: Perhaps tomorrow brings a clock that neither one can mend.
ELI: Then two apprentices can listen, and begin the work again.

songs.title: The Mechanical Orchard
lines: The factory orchard has gears in the branches,
Small silver apples and copper-leaf chances.
Rattle and clatter, a patterned procession,
A crank in the canopy catches compression.
I'm mapping the movement, examining measures,
The belt makes a loop where the old pressure settles.
A tiny brass sparrow slips loose from a line,
Its wing starts a rhythm on half-beaten time.
Click—then a flick; little wheels in a spiral,
A spring starts to sing as the pressure goes viral.
I catch it. One hand. The assembly goes still.
There isn't a manual for making things feel.
The foreman says, "Fix it; the schedule is waiting."
The bird in my palm has a windup heart skating.
I pull at the panel and loosen a pin,
The gears start a cadence then stagger again.
Too tight and it falters; too slack and it sways,
The smallest adjustment can alter the phase.
I test out the tension, attend to the timing,
The shafts make a wave with the loose bearings chiming.
My partner asks, "Why does a toy need a song?"
I tell her, "It shows us what's moving all wrong."
A dozen machines that were running in pairs
Have slipped into sync with the noise of the stairs.
I stop their conveyors. The shop falls to hush.
One little bird hums without needing to rush.
Then every brass apple starts turning in place,
And light from the skylight goes over its face.
The foreman looks down at the order he's holding,
Then leaves us an hour for careful unfolding.
We mend what was broken, not chasing perfection,
And let the bird rest by the parts of its section.

songs.title: The Last Elevator Operator
lines: The elevator opens on a floor without a name,
The operator notices the dial has changed its frame.
A woman with a suitcase says she needs the office nine,
He pushes through the numbers, but the buttons misalign.
At three, a paper airplane slides across the marble floor,
At five, the air smells faintly of the ocean near the shore.
At seven, all the mirrors hold the passengers from yesterday,
He shuts the brass accordion gate and turns his eyes away.
The woman asks him quietly, "What happened to this place?"
He points toward the empty chairs and keeps a steady face.
"The building closed at midnight, half the tenants moved last spring,
But every evening somebody pulls the cable with a string."
They pass the floor of clocks, where every hand is set to four,
A postcard from the suitcase falls and skates across the floor.
It bears a faded photograph of this same operator,
Standing by the elevator with a girl who would be later.
The operator reaches down and recognizes the coat,
The same bright checkered pattern and the message that she wrote.
The woman says, "My mother kept that picture in a drawer.
She told me if I had a question, I should try this door."
He presses nine, then pulls a key from underneath the light,
The lift climbs past the vacant floors, still glowing in the night.
An office desk is waiting with a notebook at its side,
A stack of children's drawings and a photograph inside.
The woman reads the letters; she has never seen that hand.
He says, "Your mother wrote them when she worked here, where I stand."
The strangest thing about the lift was never where it went,
But all the little keepsakes that an ordinary life had sent.
They ride back to the lobby as the morning windows shine,
And he finally paints a label on the button marked as nine.

songs.title: The Arguments of Day and Night
lines: DAY: I show the roads and rooftops where the children want to play.
NIGHT: I let their busy minds put every borrowed thought away.
DAY: Without my light the orchard never knows how it should grow.
NIGHT: Without my dark the roots forget the quiet down below.
DAY: My workers build the bridges and the painted city walls.
NIGHT: My cleaners mend the broken things when all the hammering falls.
DAY: You only bring the shadows that can swallow up the street.
NIGHT: You only bring the hurry that leaves blisters on their feet.
DAY: I hear the market opening; each shutter has a song.
NIGHT: I hear the empty kitchen where the waiter's shift ran long.
DAY: I set the open windows where the wind can find its lane.
NIGHT: I cool the crowded bedrooms after hours of summer rain.
DAY: Without the sunrise, tell me how the travelers know their way.
NIGHT: By lanterns, stars and kindness from the people where they stay.
DAY: You make the city anxious with your unfamiliar sky.
NIGHT: You make the city restless when the noon goes racing by.
DAY: Then who will mark the moment when the final bell is rung?
NIGHT: The same old clock that told us both how everything begun.
DAY: The old wall clock? Its painted hands are rusty, bent and slow.
NIGHT: And still the little baker knows exactly when to go.
DAY: Perhaps I'm not the answer to the questions that we share.
NIGHT: Perhaps I'm not the enemy of light upon the stair.
DAY: I make a shadow longer as the afternoon runs west.
NIGHT: I take that shadow gently and I let the city rest.
DAY: Tomorrow we'll exchange the roads and roofs and apple trees.
NIGHT: And I'll return the morning when the baker lights his keys.
DAY: One world cannot be daytime, or the sky would never change.
NIGHT: One world cannot be midnight, or the birds would lose their range.
BOTH: The argument was never which one deserved the sky.
BOTH: It's how we pass the morning when the evening passes by.

songs.title: The Costume Department Ghost
lines: A velvet hat went missing when the orchestra tuned up,
The tailor spilled a thimble in a lady's paper cup.
The director shouted, "Places!" and the curtain began to sway,
But somebody had hung a pirate coat where the king's was yesterday.
In the costume room the mirrors caught a flicker in the light,
A ghost in borrowed overalls was stitching through the night.
He whistled like a kettle and he danced upon a chair,
Then sewed a little pocket in a sleeve that wasn't there.
"Who keeps changing costumes?" cried the director from the wing.
The ghost replied, "The script does; I just help it learn to sing."
He gave the silent actress shoes that squeaked beneath the floor,
And dressed the timid villain as the keeper of the door.
The first act went to pieces when the king became a cook,
A knight arrived with teaspoons and a very worried look.
But every time the chaos threatened one more tangled scene,
The ghost sent out a costume that revealed what characters mean.
Put on the hat, take off the fear,
The part is only borrowed while you're here.
Pull on the coat, then step into the light,
The audience can tell when you're not hiding it tonight.
In act two, the ghost was caught with needles in his sleeve,
The director said, "I'll lock you up until you learn to leave."
The ghost said, "I was hired when this theater first began.
I've dressed a thousand people, but I never had a hand
To wave at all the others from the stage when they were done,
So I stitched a little pocket where I hid the setting sun."
The actress found the pocket and she opened it on cue,
A bundle of old playbills fell like paper petals through.
The final scene went silent; all the players took a bow,
Then made a space beside them for the ghost they could see now.
Put on the hat, take off the fear,
The part is only borrowed while you're here.
The ghost put on his own old coat and smiled beneath the light,
Then took the closing curtain home to mend it overnight.
